item.text: {"text":"Recent research supports evaluating rejection explanations against evidence rather than linguistic plausibility. [Shimizu et al. (WWW 2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13248) show that strong conventional explanation metrics do not ensure alignment with users’ positive and negative opinions; their review-derived supervision is unavailable in this task. [Polleti et al. (2025)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11257-025-09432-6) study balanced reasons for and against recommendations, supporting explicit rejection diagnostics. A [2026 preprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27789) distinguishes current demand from recommendation policies and rejection boundaries, emphasizing outcome feedback over plausible reasoning. These sources do not establish a validated taxonomy covering all five proposed dimensions.\n\nA practical synthesis is a multilabel annotation scheme: current-purpose mismatch, duplication/redundancy, incompatibility, quantity mismatch, and mood mismatch. Each recommendation-level label should include an exact supporting feedback span or metadata/history reference, evidence timestamp, and status: supported, contradicted, or unknown. Titles and descriptions can establish documented attributes; histories establish prior interactions, but cannot alone prove ownership, satisfaction, current need, desired quantity, or mood. Require explicit feedback for subjective claims. Following rationale-collection research’s emphasis on evidence and agreement ([2024 survey](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11157010/)), independently double-annotate a subset; report per-label counts, raw agreement, chance-corrected agreement, supported-label coverage, and unknown rates before adjudication. Treat this as a proposed audit protocol, not a literature-validated instrument. Keep the twenty-user full-catalog audit descriptive and separate from the fixed macro validation HR@10; it cannot establish benchmark improvement or population-wide rejection prevalence."}
